grh_5bec49813de52854e01f.title: Erminie
paragraphs: Erminie and her father's secretary Eugene are in love, but her father has already arranged for her to marry the Vicomte de Brissac. Before the nobleman can arrive, an escaped criminal robs him of his clothes and papers and enters the household under his name. Eugene's suspicions help bring soldiers to the scene, and the real vicomte arrives in time to expose the impostor and see the love between Erminie and Eugene. He releases Erminie from the arranged engagement, allowing her father to approve the match she truly wants.

Lee as radio adaptor, Gordon MacRae as host, and Marvin Miller as announcer.
The surviving recording runs about 30 minutes. The broadcast is also associated with [[org|org.f7185f50dd01455d|Association of American Railroads]].
This version dramatizes [[work|work.rr.3b81fabc9c7b5c3a|Erminie]]. Jerome Lawrence adapted it for radio and Robert E. Lee adapted it for radio.

grh_5bc8f7cde4016ac860bf.title: I Want Him Dead
paragraphs: After his young son Billy is killed when he rides his bicycle into the path of Robert Trenton's car, George Green becomes consumed by the belief that Trenton was drunk and escaped justice. His obsession with revenge drives away his wife and daughter and costs him his job, until he takes a gun to Trenton's home intending to kill him. Trenton reveals that he has an inoperable brain tumor and that what looked like drunkenness was a seizure; Billy's death was an unavoidable accident. Confronted with the truth and with a man already facing death, George puts away the gun and calls his wife to say he is coming home.

grh_5b5ffcb3e7dd62aad05d.title: Take a Letter Darling
paragraphs: Advertising executive A.M. MacGregor hires artist Tom Verney as her male secretary because his charm can help her manage difficult male clients and their jealous wives. Tom accepts only to earn money for a painting trip to Mexico, but the unusual arrangement becomes personal as the two fall in love while insisting they are too independent for romance.
